analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance plan sold alongside private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: The public health insurance option died in committee: it was introduced in January 2017, referred to the Senate health committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The CHOICE Act would have created a new government health insurance plan, sold on the same marketplaces as private plans and required to follow the same rules. Premiums would have to cover the plan's own costs, and the government would negotiate doctor, hospital, and drug prices, falling back to Medicare rates if no deal was reached. Most doctors and hospitals already in Medicare would be in the plan automatically unless they opted out.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying coverage on the ACA exchanges, including the self-employed, small-business workers, and anyone without job-based insurance. They would get a new, lower-cost plan option to choose from, with rates set to cover costs rather than insurer profit margins, and their premiums could fall as the public plan pressured private insurers to compete.

how_it_helps.text: HHS must offer a public health insurance option as a qualified health plan throughout the United States, with bronze, silver, and gold tiers, giving exchange shoppers a government-run alternative to private plans [S2][S3].

The plan must set premiums at a level sufficient to fully finance its own benefits and administrative costs, so it competes on price rather than relying on a subsidy private plans do not get [S2][S3].
HHS must negotiate provider and prescription drug rates, and if negotiation fails, pay at Medicare fee-for-service rates, which are generally lower than what private insurers pay [S2][S3].
Providers participating in Medicare or Medicaid are automatically in the plan unless they opt out, so the public plan would start with a broad nationwide network rather than a thin one [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers, which would face a government competitor for exchange customers. Hospitals and doctors would face reimbursement pressure, since the public plan defaults to Medicare rates if negotiations fail. Brand-name drug makers would face government-negotiated prices. Taxpayers would front a one-time startup fund for the plan's reserves, which the plan must repay over ten years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires provider participation by default: any Medicare or Medicaid provider is in the public plan unless they opt out, which hospitals and physician groups objected to as government coercion of their rates [S3].
The public option would only be sold on the exchanges, so people with employer-based coverage, the majority of insured Americans, would not benefit directly [S2][S3].

Falling back to Medicare rates if negotiations fail could push some providers to drop the plan, limiting the network and access in some areas; the bill acknowledges this by requiring rate modifications for services Medicare does not cover [S3].

The plan must be fully self-financing through premiums with only a repayable startup fund, so in its early years it would have less cushion than private insurers backed by large parent companies, and could struggle if enrollment was low [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people stuck buying exchange coverage at rising premiums, a cheaper government-run plan with a broad network is a substantial benefit, and the cost is borne mainly by insurers and providers who would earn less per patient. The honest objections are about design, not principle: default provider participation is a blunt tool, and restricting the plan to the exchanges leaves most Americans out. On balance, for the population it covers, the benefits clearly outweigh the costs, which fall on concentrated interests rather than taxpayers beyond a repayable startup fund.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the CHOICE Act on January 23, 2017, joined by Sens. Sherrod Brown and Al Franken [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced, and no further action was taken [S5].
Thirteen Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still in committee, so it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, hospital systems, and brand-name drug makers are better off because the bill died without a vote: no government plan competes with them for exchange customers, and no negotiated Medicare-benchmark rates constrain what they are paid. People paying high exchange premiums get no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic, one sponsor and thirteen cosponsors with no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican majority that controlled the Senate health committee never acted on it.

industries.note: A government-run plan on the same exchanges, priced to cover costs rather than profit, would compete directly for their customers and pressure their premiums down. Their gain from the bill's defeat is ordinary people's continued exposure to rising exchange premiums.

The public plan would pay negotiated rates, defaulting to Medicare rates if no deal is reached, which are typically below private insurance rates. Medicare and Medicaid providers would be in the plan automatically unless they opted out.
Drug prices under the public plan would be set by negotiated rates, falling back to Medicare fee-for-service rates, ending their ability to charge the public plan whatever private plans accept.

industries.industry: Health insurance brokers and exchange intermediaries
industries.note: The bill routes the new public plan through the existing ACA exchange structure and qualifies it as a standard qualified health plan, keeping the exchange marketplace and its subsidy machinery as the permanent channel for subsidized coverage.
